title: What Zen is not
hookLine: not just calm, not just paradox: a whole way with ethics, ritual and community

cards: A scented candle with zen on the label. A tea called zen. A spa, a phone app, a paint color, all promising zen.
In everyday English it's come to mean relaxed, unbothered, nothing getting to you. Meanwhile, in a Zen temple, the day may begin before dawn with bowing and chanting. People recite vows together.
The floors get scrubbed. A meal is eaten from a set of bowls in a set order. And the teacher expects everyone to keep the precepts.
Calm may be in there somewhere. It isn't the whole picture.

teach.b: First, Zen is not just calm. Calm can come from sitting, and nobody turns it away.
But look where this block kept pointing: the herdsman rides home, then walks back into the market; the meal is eaten from nested bowls, just enough, every bowl cleaned.
Zen points at seeing clearly, and that includes the moments that aren't calm at all.
Second, Zen is not just paradox. Koans like the stone bridge or three pounds of flax get passed around for their strangeness.
But a koan lives inside a relationship: a student, a teacher, a meeting room, many hours on the cushion. Pulled out alone, it looks like a riddle. Inside the practice, it's work.
Third, ethics. Zen communities hold a ceremony for receiving the precepts, jukai in Japanese, where people vow not to kill, not to steal, not to lie, and more.

The precepts are the floor the cushion sits on. An old verse in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
Notice the order: purifying the mind comes last, after not harming and doing good.
Fourth, ritual and community: bowing, chanting, robes, bells, shared meals, people sitting side by side week after week.
Strip those away and what's left is the word on the candle. Keep them, and Zen is a whole way of living with others, with sitting at its center.

how: Zen communities keep the precepts alongside sitting: in a ceremony called jukai in Japanese, practitioners formally receive vows such as not killing, not stealing and not lying, and daily life in a Zen temple includes bowing, chanting, work and meals taken together.

games.q: what does “what zen is not” mean?
o: Zen is more than calm: precepts, ritual and community too
Zen is mainly paradox: riddles meant to confuse the mind
Zen is relaxation, a way to stay calm and unbothered

games.q: what Zen is not: tap the pairs.
p: no sin, do good, purify the mind

s: calm is welcome, but Zen is a whole way with precepts, ritual and community.
Zen communities hold a ceremony for receiving the precepts
it's called jukai in Japanese: vows not to kill, steal or lie, and more.
a koan is a riddle meant to be solved alone
a koan lives inside a relationship with a teacher and long hours of sitting.

games.q: a friend says, "zen? that's just about staying calm." which answer fits what you heard today?
o: yes, calm is the whole of it.
calm is part of it, inside precepts, ritual and community.
no, zen is only about strange paradoxes.
games.why: Zen practice holds sitting inside a larger life: keeping precepts, bowing and chanting, working and eating with others.

practice: Choose one precept to hold for a few breaths: not killing, like carrying a spider outside; not stealing, like not taking credit that isn't yours; or not lying, even the small polite untruths.
Then sit with it, the way someone receiving precepts might, breathing in and out and holding the choice quietly.

wordCard.voice: What Zen is not: not only calm, and not only paradox. A whole way, with precepts, ritual and community, and sitting at its center. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: jukai, receiving the precepts, a ceremony held in Zen communities.

carryVoice: Your line: more than calm. Precepts, ritual and people, with the cushion at the center. Week done.
